content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
I like the regularization about diversifying the weights in the convolution layers. The main contribution of this paper is to design the better optimization algorithm for compressive Compressive Hyperspherical energy. The difficulty lies in that the dimension is too high. So this paper propose to adopt two dimension reduction schemes: random project and angle-preserving projection. The whole algorithms are clear and easy to understand. Experimental results also demonstrate that the algorithms are effective and get better results in various problems. 

There is theoretical analysis about angle preservation for the projection algorithms. And there are also statistical insights. The theoretical and statistical  analysis should be correct though I did not check them completely. However, the analysis seems not related to network. And I am wondering how the projection helps optimize the networks. This will strengthen the quality of this paper.

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
Thank you for your appreciation on our work. Our analysis focuses on the general effects of the regularization, which is independent of our network structure. By arguing the hyperspherical diversity can help the generalization ability, we analyze how well our proposed regularization can achieve such goal.

The intuition that the projection can help to optimize the hyperspherical energy is inspired by the simulated annealing where randomness can improve the solution by avoiding bad local minima. Running gradient descent on the current MHE regularization yields a static update rule, which is difficult to run away from bad local minima. With the dynamic projection (i.e., random projection or optimization-based projection), the update rule also becomes dynamic in every iteration. We show that random projection is one well-performing way to transform the static MHE regularization to a dynamic regularization.

It brings up an important contribution we make in the paper. For the explicit regularization on weights, CoMHE is one of the first methods that introduces dynamic regularization, which is different from the previous static MHE regularization and orthogonal regularization in the sense that CoMHE regularizes the network dynamically based on different projection matrices.

As for the question “how the projection helps optimize the networks”, we agree with the reviewer that analysis on this issue will strengthen our paper. Considering a neural network with CoMHE regularization, it is a highly non-convex and nonlinear optimization and is difficult to analyze. Some related theoretical results are given in [Implicit regularization in matrix factorization, NeurIPS 2017]. Since it will be a much more involved analysis, we leave it for future investigation.

Our reasoning of why the project helps to optimize the networks follows the logic below: 

(1) We argue minimum hyperspherical diversity is an effective inductive bias that helps the neural networks generalize better. This is based on the empirical study in MHE [Learning towards Minimum Hyperspherical Energy, NeurIPS 2018] and the theoretical evidence in [Diverse Neural Network Learns True Target Functions, AISTATS 2017]. So the main question we consider in the paper is how to effectively minimize the hyperspherical energy.

(2) We show that using a random and learnable projection can better minimize the hyperspherical energy than the original MHE. Our intuition (mentioned above) and theoretical analysis also partially justifies why projection helps to optimize hyperspherical energy. Most importantly, our empirical results can validate the superiority of using projections in MHE.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
This paper presents a method for regularizing neural network weights which encourages diversity in a layer’s activations. The regularizer is motivated by encouraging the weight vectors to be uniformly distributed on the hyper-sphere. This is a challenging optimization problem which can get stuck in many local minima. The authors propose a way to avoid many of the known issues with this regularizer by projecting the weight vectors down to a lower dimension where the optimization problem is less susceptible to getting stuck in a local minima. The authors propose multiple ways to project the weight vectors to lower dimensions with random and learned projections. The authors motivate the validity of their approach by providing some theoretical guarantees that by minimizing the hyper-spherical energy (HSE) in the projected space, they are minimizing the HSE in the weight space. Further, the authors explore each approach and compare their proposed hyper-spherical regularizer to prior work and find it performs favorably. 

While I am not an expert in this specific area, I would vote overall to reject this paper.  While the authors present a through comparison of their method to other hyper-spherical regularization methods, I felt that there was an insufficient comparison to other regularization methods. I do not feel the experimental results demonstrated the benefit of the author’s approach over other HSE regularization methods and more traditional forms of regularization. 

I feel the paper could be greatly improved if the authors provided a comparison with more common regularizers. They provide a convincing demonstration that their method performs better than other HSE-based regularizers, but they do not provide much of a reference for how these methods compare in general to other types of weight regularization, so it is hard to tell from the results here that this improvement is significant. 

A main argument for the use of hyper-spherical regularization methods is their generality to be used across domains and while the authors did show this in image and point-cloud classification, their comparison was limited only to other hyper-spherical regularization methods, so again it is unclear how the proposed method compares to simpler regularizers such as a well-tuned l1/l2 or orthogonality regularizer. 

Specifically on the CIFAR10/CIFAR100 datasets, the difference in performance between the reported HSE methods is less than the difference in performance observed between minor architecture changes in the Wide Residual Networks paper (a strong model for these problems), so I was not convinced of the benefit of this method of regularization as opposed to minor architectural or hyper-parameter tweaks to standard methods.

If the authors were to provide a more thorough comparison with simpler forms for regularization and demonstrated that their method provides a significant performance boost, then I could be convinced to change my score.

content.title: Response to Review #3
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive comments and useful suggestions. We sincerely hope our response can address the reviewer’s concerns.

** Question: Comparison to more common regularizers

** Response:  Thank you for the suggestion. MHE is one of the most well-performing regularizations in the current literatures. Outperforming MHE by a large margin shows that our method actually achieves the state-of-the-art performance. In MHE’s original paper [1], they show that MHE can consistently and significantly outperform classic regularizations like orthogonal.

Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we still conduct experiments to compare with L1, L1+L2, orthogonal, and SRIP [2] on CIFAR-100. Note that, we use the best hyperparameter setup for all the compared methods. The hyperparameters are selected using cross-validation. If not otherwise specified, L2 is used as default for all the methods, since some methods like orthogonal regularization are difficult to converge without L2 weight decay. Note that L2 weight decay is used in all the methods in the paper as well. One can see that L2 weight decay penalizes the norm of the weights, while our CoMHE regularizes the direction (i.e., angle) of the weights.

----------------------------------------
Method             Test Error (%)  
----------------------------------------
Baseline                 28.03   
---------------------------------------
L1 (without L2)      31.48
---------------------------------------
L1+L2                      27.40
---------------------------------------
Orthogonal           27.01
---------------------------------------
SRIP [2]                  25.80
---------------------------------------
HS-MHE [1]           25.96
---------------------------------------
RP-CoMHE            24.39
---------------------------------------
AP-CoMHE            24.33
---------------------------------------

Moreover, in our paper, we actually have already compared to two classic orthogonal regularizations on ImageNet (Table 8 in the main paper).

[1] Liu, Lin, Liu, Liu, Yu, Dai, Song. Learning towards Minimum Hyperspherical Energy, NeurIPS 2018
[2] Bansal, Chen, Wang. Can We Gain More from Orthogonality Regularizations in Training Deep CNNs?, NeurIPS 2018

** Question: Specifically on the CIFAR10/CIFAR100 datasets, the difference in performance between the reported HSE methods is less than the difference in performance observed between minor architecture changes in the Wide Residual Networks paper (a strong model for these problems), so I was not convinced of the benefit of this method of regularization as opposed to minor architectural or hyper-parameter tweaks to standard methods.

** Response: One of the biggest difference between architecture changes and regularization is that wider and deeper networks will dramatically increase the inference time and also consume much more GPU memory, while our regularization method will NOT affect the inference speed and consumed GPU memory of the original architecture. In other words, using regularization to improve performance is more like a “free lunch”.

Moreover, the regularization method can be used simultaneously with these architecture changes, and CoMHE will produce significant gain even after these architecture changes. For example, we have shown (in Table 4&5) that on deeper and wider plain VGG-like CNNs, CoMHE can still consistently improve the performance of these networks. And we further show (in Table 7) that CoMHE can also improve the accuracy on Residual Networks. Most interestingly, the gain achieved by our CoMHE regularization is more than the gain achieved by increasing ResNet to 1001 layers.

** Summary
We agree with the reviewer that comparing to more standard regularizations could strengthen the paper. Due to the time constraint, we only provide comparison on CIFAR-100 in rebuttal. We will further conduct experiments on ImageNet and supplement the results to revision. We sincerely thank the reviewer for these great suggestions to improve our experiments.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper extends previous work on using a hyperspherical energy function for regularizing neural networks, an apporach called minimum hyperspherical energy (MHE). The authors point out several problems with optimizing the original MHE objective in high dimensions and propose the compressive minium hyperspherical energy (CoMHE) to address these problems. The main idea is to project the network weights to a lower-dimensional space and then apply the original MHE approach to the projected weights. The paper proposes numerous different ways to perform these projections, where the two main variants are based on random projects and angle preserving projections. The paper provides a number of theoretical results, showing that these projections approximately preserve the angles between pairs of weight vectors. The paper has a comprehensive experimental section, where the authors empirically evaluate the different variants of CoMHE, and they compare CoMHE based models to state-of-the-art models on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet. Most considerable, with a plain 9-layer CNN they obtain close to a 2 percentage point improvement over ResNet-1001 on CIFAR-100.

On the positive side, the paper is well written and easy to follow. The paper both investigates the theoretical aspects of the proposed methodology and has comprehensives empirical evaluation. In particular, many of the reported results are comparable to the state-of-the-art, showing that this is effective regularization approach that gives good generalization.

The main shortcoming of the papers is that while it contains many new methodological contributions, the paper appears to be somewhat incremental work. Furthermore, while the experimental results are comprehensive, it appears that only for figure 1, multiple training-runs have been performed. When standard deviation over multiple runs is not reported, it makes it hard to draw conclusions from the reported results. For instance, are there any significant differences between the results reported in table 2, or does the table show that the methods are not sensitive to the dimension of the projection?

Given these shortcomings, I recommend a weak reject of the paper.

To clarify my understanding of the paper, I would like the authors to answer the following questions:

(1) How can you conclude that your empirical results do not show any noticeable performance gain with using multiple projects for AP-CoMHE when you only report the result for one project in table 3?

(2) In table 4, I do not understand why you did not increase t even further.  When do you start to see overfitting? Could the baseline archive the same performance as the other models with a larger t?

(3) On the top of page 2, you write "Third, when the number of neurons is smaller than the dimension of the space (it is often the case in neural networks), MHE defines an ill-posed problem because the neurons can not even fully occupy the space." I do not understand which "space" you refer to here. Could you please clarify this?

content.title: Response to Review #4 (part 1)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions and the effort to help us improve the paper. We treat the reviewer's every concern very seriously and address them carefully. We truly hope our response can clarify the reviewer's concerns.

** Question: When standard deviation over multiple runs is not reported, it makes it hard to draw conclusions from the reported results. For instance, are there any significant differences between the results reported in table 2, or does the table show that the methods are not sensitive to the dimension of the projection?

** Response: Thank you for the suggestion. The standard deviation for Table is given as follows:

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Projection Dim                 10                   20                 30                   40                  80         
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RP-CoMHE              25.48±0.12    25.32±0.10    24.60±0.07     24.75±0.05    25.46±0.05 
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AP-CoMHE(alter.)    25.21±0.04    24.60±0.03    24.95±0.02     24.97±0.04    24.99±0.05
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AP-CoMHE(unroll.)  25.32±0.02    24.59±0.02    24.33±0.03     24.93±0.04    25.12±0.03
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The standard deviation is in fact quite small, and the performance gain is statistically significant. This table shows that no matter which value we pick for the projection dimension, both RP-CoMHE and AP-CoMHE can consistently outperform Half-space MHE (25.96%) by a considerable margin (experiments are conducted with the same setting as Half-space MHE). 

Moreover, we empirically find that setting the projection dimension to the range between 25-50 can achieve the best performance. Such range also shows that CoMHE is not very sensitive to projection dimension and the projection dimension is very easy to pick. 

The standard deviation of all the results presented in the paper is around 0.04 (with 0.12 being the maximum), which also means that our results can be reproduced very easily. We will add the standard deviation to all results in the paper.

** Question: How can you conclude that your empirical results do not show any noticeable performance gain with using multiple projects for AP-CoMHE when you only report the result for one project in table 3?

** Response: First of all, AP-CoMHE does not need to use multiple projection by nature, since its projection matrix is learned with a specific objective function rather than being random. In fact, we have also experimented multiple projections in AP-CoMHE, and we show the performance below to validate our point:

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Projections           1                    5                     10                     20                   30                     80
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AP-CoMHE     24.33±0.05    24.30±0.04     24.35±0.06     24.38±0.05    24.52±0.04     24.55±0.03
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Because using multiple projections reduce the training speed and will take more GPU memory, we generally don’t use multiple projections in AP-CoMHE since it does not have obvious gain.

content.title: Response to Review #4 (part 2)
content.comment:
** Question: In table 4, I do not understand why you did not increase t even further.  When do you start to see overfitting? Could the baseline archive the same performance as the other models with a larger t?

** Response: In fact, the reason we did not increase t further is due to the lack of GPU memory. We use RTX 2080 Ti with 11 GB memory. t=16 is almost the maximum number. We use a Titan Xp with 12 GB memory to run the experiment with t=20 (t=20 the maximum number we can run on a Titan Xp). The results are shown as follows:

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Method                 Baseline              HS-MHE               RP-CoMHE             AP-CoMHE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Accuracy            23.77±0.06           21.22±0.05            20.62±0.06              20.50±0.03    
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As the experimental results show, CoMHE can still significantly improve the baseline. In fact, we find that with wider and deeper networks, CoMHE can achieve more significant performance gain. It may partially because wider and deeper networks will have more redundant filters, leading to ineffective usage of filters. More notably, with deep networks (for example 15-layer plain CNN as in Table 5), the baseline network can not converge while our CoMHE can help the network converge to a good local minima.

As a result, we can find that even using a larger t, the performance baseline is still significantly lower than CoMHE.

** Question: On the top of page 2, you write "Third, when the number of neurons is smaller than the dimension of the space (it is often the case in neural networks), MHE defines an ill-posed problem because the neurons can not even fully occupy the space." I do not understand which "space" you refer to here. Could you please clarify this?

** Response: For example, we consider a convolution layer with 128 neurons (i.e., convolution kernels) with dimension 3x3x64 each. These numbers are very common in a typical CNN, so it is a practical convolution layer. In this case, the dimension that each neuron lives in is 576, which is much larger than the number of neurons (i.e., 128). Therefore, these neurons can not fully represent the full space (dimension 576), and they can only represent a subspace of dimension 128. In this case, the problem that the original MHE defines is ill-posed, since making 128 neurons diverse in 576 dimensional space is very trivial. However, if we can optimize MHE in a low-dimensional space whose dimension is lower than 128, then the problem becomes more meaningful and the solution will be nontrivial.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review: The paper builds on the hyperspherical energy minimization line of research and proposes that instead of optimizing the distance between actual filters (or network parameters) it optimizes the distance between a projection of the filters (or network parameters). The idea is quite straightforward. Nevertheless, I do not fully understand the rationale behind it. Also, the developed theory is a straightforward application of well-known theorems and lemmas of random projections. There is a variety of experiments showing negligible performance improvement.

content.title: Response to Review #2
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the comments. We hope our response can clarify your concerns.

** Question: I do not fully understand the rationale behind it (CoMHE)

** Response: As our paper has mentioned, CoMHE is motivated by the drawbacks of MHE. The optimization of MHE in high-dimensional space is very challenging: the gradients of MHE get very small when the neurons are roughly diverse. In high-dimensional space, the neurons tend to be diverse. (For details, refer to the third paragraph in the introduction) To address these shortcomings, CoMHE will optimize the hyperspherical energy in a projected low-dimensional space.

Our intuition behind CoMHE is that introducing randomness in MHE could be beneficial the neural network’s generalizability, since the static MHE regularization on neurons is easily stuck in local minima and has little regularization effect as the training goes on. As an analogy, our projections (random, angle-preserving, adversarial, etc.) here serve a similar role to simulated annealing that can help the solution escape some bad local minima.

As another important contribution, CoMHE is a dynamic regularization, in contrast to the original MHE regularization. For the explicit regularization on weights (e.g., orthogonal regularization, original MHE regularization, etc.), CoMHE is one of the first methods that introduces dynamic regularization, which is different from the existing regularizations in the sense that CoMHE regularizes the neurons dynamically based on different projection matrices. That is to say, the equivalent form of CoMHE in each iteration can be different and the regularization effect in each iteration is dynamic.

** Question: There is a variety of experiments showing negligible performance improvement.

** Response: With all due respect, we disagree with the reviewer that our performance gain is negligible. CoMHE is able to outperform the previous state-of-the-art MHE regularization with 1%-2% on CIFAR, 0.5%-1% (top-1) on ImageNet and ~0.5% on PointNet. Compared to the baseline, the improvement is even larger. To get a sense of how significant that improving 0.5%-1% on ImageNet, we show some well-known experimental results: From ResNet-34 to ResNet-50, the top-1 error is improved by ~0.7%; From ResNet-101 to ResNet-152,  the top-1 error is improved by ~0.4%. Improving 0.5% top-1 error on ImageNet is already considered as significant.

We will appreciate it if the reviewer can elaborate the concerns in detail and what we can do to improve our paper.
